Non-normal Limits and Joint Calibration of Cross-fitted Heterogeneity Tests

Even He ††thanks: Email: heyiwen5@gmail.com Affiliation: College of Science, Inner Mongolia University of Technology, Hohhot 010051, China    Zaizai Yan ††thanks: Email: zz.yan@163.com Affiliation: College of Science, Inner Mongolia University of Technology, Hohhot 010051, China
Abstract

Cross-fitting is used to test whether a ranking learned in a randomized experiment separates units that benefit from treatment from those that do not: each fold is ranked by a model fitted to the other folds, and the standardized difference in estimated effects between units ranked high and low is compared with a normal distribution. Under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity the ranking is determined by noise, and because each fold helps to rank the others the fold estimates are dependent. We show that this dependence changes the shape of the null distribution, not just its variance. For least squares on one covariate the limit is bimodal for two folds and skewed for many, no variance correction restores the level, and the model is a counterexample to a published central limit theorem. With many covariates the limit approaches normality, but its variance stays inflated. Removing the non-normal component of the statistic removes its power, so we keep the statistic and change its reference distribution: joint calibration simulates together the moments that choose the rankings and those that evaluate them and applies the same selection to the draws; it has asymptotically exact level and requires no refitting. Applications to clinical and marketing trials, together with random treatment reassignments on their covariates, demonstrate that the standard test substantially inflates Type I error and can produce spurious rejections that joint calibration avoids.

Keywords: Cross-fitting; Heterogeneous treatment effect; Joint calibration; Non-normal limit; Randomized experiment.

1 Introduction

Randomized experiments are increasingly analysed with rankings learned by machine learning: a model of the conditional average treatment effect, such as a causal forest or a metalearner (Athey and Imbens, 2016; Wager and Athey, 2018; Künzel et al., 2019; Nie and Wager, 2021), is fitted to part of the data and used to order the remaining units by predicted benefit. Sorted group average treatment effects (Chernozhukov et al., 2025; Imai and Li, 2025a) ask whether such a ranking separates units that benefit from units that do not, by comparing the average effects of the units ranked above and below the median. To avoid evaluating a ranking on the data that produced it, the data are split (Cox, 1975): the sample is divided into folds, the ranking applied to each fold is learned from other folds, and the fold estimates are averaged. The standardized average is then compared with a normal distribution.

For a fixed target this comparison is justified. With orthogonal scores, the estimate from each fold is asymptotically linear in an influence function that does not depend on the training data, so the fold estimates are asymptotically independent and their average is asymptotically normal (Chernozhukov et al., 2018; Chernozhukov et al., 2023). The null hypothesis of no heterogeneity breaks the argument. If every unit has the same conditional average treatment effect, every ranking is optimal, and the value of the optimal ranking is not a differentiable functional of the distribution of the data (Hirano and Porter, 2012; Luedtke and van der Laan, 2016); the test error of a learned classifier has the same property (Laber and Murphy, 2011). A consistent learner converges to a constant function, but its estimation error still decides which half of a fold is called the high-effect group, so the learned ranking is determined by noise. In the usual design, in which each fold is ranked by a model fitted to all the other folds, the noise of one fold helps to choose the ranking applied to another, and conversely. Each fold estimate still has mean zero given its ranking, but the fold estimates are no longer independent.

We show that this dependence changes the shape of the limiting distribution, not only its variance. The analysis does not rest on the causal setting: it applies whenever some folds choose, through a fixed number of their sample moments, the weights with which another fold is evaluated, and the evaluation has mean zero under the null hypothesis whatever weights are chosen. We call the moments of a fold that help to choose rankings its training moments, and those to which a ranking is applied its evaluation moments. Conditionally on the training moments, the limit is normal. Unconditionally it is the sum of a normal variable and a non-normal one, weighted by the correlation between the training and evaluation moments of a fold; it is normal when this correlation is zero and, in the linear models that we study, only then. The non-normal component cannot simply be removed, because it is the component that a signal shifts: a statistic without it has a normal limit but no power against the alternatives that the learner is designed to detect.

For least squares on one covariate the limit is explicit. With two folds its density has a closed form and is bimodal, with many folds it is skewed, and standardizing by the exact variance does not restore the nominal level; the best linear predictor test, in which the two moments coincide, rejects almost twice as often as it should with two folds. This model satisfies the conditions of Theorem 6 of Imai and Li (2025a), which asserts asymptotic normality of the standardized group effect, and is therefore a counterexample to it. With many covariates the limit approaches normality while its variance stays inflated by a factor that does not decrease with the number of folds. The variance corrections of the cross-validation literature err in either direction, depending on the numbers of covariates and folds, whereas a correction estimated from the training and evaluation moments restores the level when the covariates are many. Under local alternatives the limit stays non-normal, and the strength of signal at which normality returns cannot be estimated consistently. The same structure yields a test, joint calibration: a parametric bootstrap that draws the training and evaluation moments jointly from their estimated normal distribution and applies the selection to the draws. Its level is asymptotically exact, whichever folds train each ranking, and it requires no refitting of the learner.

The dependence of cross-validation folds is well known. Resampled tt-tests over-reject (Dietterich, 1998), corrections based on moments allow for training sets that overlap (Nadeau and Bengio, 2003; Markatou et al., 2005), the variance of KK-fold cross-validation has no estimator that is unbiased under every distribution (Bengio and Grandvalet, 2004), nested cross-validation repairs intervals for prediction error (Bates et al., 2024), and central limit theorems for cross-validated risk hold under stability conditions (Austern and Zhou, 2025; Bayle et al., 2020), which even two stable learners can violate when they are compared (Bayle et al., 2026). These results concern the variance of a cross-validated estimate; here the shape changes as well, and the stability they assume fails under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity. Fava (2025) proves a central limit theorem for averages over splits that requires only convergence of the learned model, and notes that normal intervals can fail when the model converges to a constant, as it does here; we describe the limit in that case and calibrate the test.

A single split gives valid inference for the target it selects, and conditional separations can calibrate post-reduction confidence sets (Rinaldo et al., 2019; García Rasines and Young, 2023; Battey et al., 2026); pp-values from many splits can also be combined (Meinshausen et al., 2009; DiCiccio et al., 2020), whereas cross-fitting uses every fold in both roles. Tests of heterogeneity that learn no ranking (Crump et al., 2008; Ding et al., 2016) and evaluations of a ranking on held-out data (Yadlowsky et al., 2025) avoid the dependence. Kim and Ramdas (2024) found a non-normal limit when two halves of a sample swap the roles of choosing a direction and evaluating it, and Guo and Shah (2025) used this example to motivate rank-transformed subsampling; after rescaling, that limit is the member of our family in which the training and evaluation moments are perfectly correlated. Imai and Li (2025b) recommend the cross-fitted estimator of group effects with a variance that accounts for training and evaluating on the same data, through a lemma of Nadeau and Bengio (2003), and a normal interval. Under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity and with few covariates, our results imply that such an interval is not valid even with the exact variance. Wager (2025) evaluates each fold only with rankings trained on earlier folds; we keep the usual statistic and replace its reference distribution.

2 Cross-fitted tests and their limit

2.1 Setting and the usual test

We observe independent copies (Xi,Ai,Yi)(X_{i},A_{i},Y_{i}) (i=1,…,n)(i=1,\ldots,n) of covariates XX, a binary treatment AA assigned with known probability pp independently of XX, and an outcome Y=A​Y​(1)+(1−A)​Y​(0)Y=AY(1)+(1-A)Y(0), with no interference between units. 2.2 Training and evaluation moments

To see why the limit need not be normal, separate the moments that choose a ranking from those that evaluate it. Take first the simplest learner, least squares of Y~\tilde{Y} on one covariate. Fold kk is ranked by xx times the sign of the slope fitted on its training folds, and because the denominator of the slope is positive, that sign is the sign of ∑r∈F⁡(k)Pr​{(x−Pr​x)​Y~}\sum_{r\in F(k)}P_{r}\{(x-P_{r}x)\tilde{Y}\}. Each training fold rr thus contributes a single number, its training moment Pr​{(x−Pr​x)​Y~}P_{r}\{(x-P_{r}x)\tilde{Y}\}, and its treatments and outcomes reach the ranking in no other way. Fold kk is in turn evaluated through a single number, its evaluation moment Pk​(g​Y~)P_{k}(g\tilde{Y}), where gg is the median split of xx. Every fold therefore plays two roles, each through one moment, and the two moments of a fold are correlated because they multiply the same outcomes.

The general setting keeps this structure and has three ingredients. The first is a feature map h:𝒳→ℝdh:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, whose moments train the rankings. The second is a set of JJ candidate rankings, each represented by a bounded weight gjg_{j} with mean zero under the distribution of XX; the moments of these weights evaluate a fold. Median splits on single covariates are an example, and contrasts between the top and bottom quintile groups of a covariate, as in Chernozhukov et al. (2025), are another once the quantile conditions of § S4.1 are imposed at each threshold. The third is a selection function ω:ℝd→ℝJ\omega:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{J}, bounded and unchanged by positive rescaling of its argument, which turns the summed training moments into a weight on each candidate; for instance, ω\omega may select the candidate with the largest absolute training moment, with its sign. The example above has h⁡(x)=xh(x)=x, J=1J=1, g1​(x)=sign​(x)g_{1}(x)=\mathrm{sign}(x) and ω⁡(z)=sign⁡(z)\omega(z)=\mathrm{sign}(z).

Let ν=Y~−τ\nu=\tilde{Y}-\tau,

V=[{h⁡(X)−E​h​(X)}T​ν,g1​(X)​ν,…,gJ​(X)​ν]T,Σ=E⁡(V​VT),V=\bigl[\{h(X)-Eh(X)\}^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}\nu,\ g_{1}(X)\nu,\ \ldots,\ g_{J}(X)\nu\bigr]^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}},\qquad\Sigma=E(VV^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}),

and partition Σ\Sigma into blocks ΣZ​Z\Sigma_{ZZ}, ΣZ​U=ΣU​ZT\Sigma_{ZU}=\Sigma_{UZ}^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}} and ΣU​U\Sigma_{UU} of sizes dd and JJ. 2.3 A general limit

Theorem 1.

Suppose that the null hypothesis holds, that E⁡[{1+‖h⁡(X)‖2}​(1+ν2)]<∞E[\{1+\|h(X)\|^{2}\}(1+\nu^{2})]<\infty, that KK, dd and JJ are fixed, that the quantile conditions of § S4.1 hold, and that Σ^U​U\hat{\Sigma}_{UU} converges in probability to ΣU​U\Sigma_{UU}. Let (ZkT,UkT)T(Z_{k}^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}},U_{k}^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}})^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}} (k=1,…,K)(k=1,\ldots,K) be independent N⁡(0,Σ)N(0,\Sigma) vectors, ωk=ω⁡(∑r∈F⁡(k)Zr)\omega_{k}=\omega(\sum_{r\in F(k)}Z_{r}) and v=K−1​∑kωkT​ΣU​U​ωkv=K^{-1}\sum_{k}\omega_{k}^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}\Sigma_{UU}\omega_{k}. If, with probability one, v>0v>0 and ω\omega is continuous at each ∑r∈F⁡(k)Zr\sum_{r\in F(k)}Z_{r}, then TnT_{n} converges in distribution to

TΣ=(Kv)−1/2∑k=1KωkTUk.T_{\Sigma}=(Kv)^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\omega_{k}^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}U_{k}. (2)

The proof in § S4.2 combines a joint central limit theorem for the moments of all folds with the continuous mapping theorem. The limit keeps the selection step: the Gaussian vectors pass through the same function ω\omega as the data. Theorem 1 therefore covers every ranking that is chosen from finitely many candidates and depends on the treatments and outcomes of its training folds only through a fixed number of moments: least squares on one covariate, a choice among the median splits of several covariates by their training moments, and combinations of the two. Least squares on several covariates chooses from a continuum of rankings and is treated in § 3.3. Nor is the theorem specific to treatment effects. The null hypothesis enters only through E⁡(ν∣X)=0E(\nu\mid X)=0, and the treatment only through the transformed outcome, so the same limit governs any cross-fitted statistic in which training folds choose, through a fixed number of moments, the weights with which another fold is evaluated, provided that the evaluation has mean zero under the null hypothesis whatever weights are chosen. The cross U-statistic of Kim and Ramdas (2024) is one instance outside the causal setting.

Proof.

Given the training moments, Uk=Γ​Zk+EkU_{k}=\Gamma Z_{k}+E_{k}, where E1,…,EKE_{1},\ldots,E_{K} are independent N⁡(0,ΣU​U−Γ​ΣZ​U)N(0,\Sigma_{UU}-\Gamma\Sigma_{ZU}) vectors independent of Z1,…,ZKZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{K}, and ω1,…,ωK\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{K} and vv are functions of Z1,…,ZKZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{K}. The conditional mean and variance follow, and they equal 00 and 11 when ΣZ​U=0\Sigma_{ZU}=0. ∎

Proposition 1 locates the non-normality. Given the training moments, the part of the evaluation moments that is uncorrelated with them contributes a normal variable, whatever rankings are chosen. The remainder, μ\mu, collects the part of each fold’s evaluation moments that its own training moment predicts, weighted by the ranking that the other folds chose for it. Each ZkZ_{k} thus enters TΣT_{\Sigma} twice, through its own term in μ\mu and through the rankings of the folds that fold kk trains, and integrating over the training moments gives a mixture of normal distributions whose means and variances depend on the rankings. Normality does not require the selection to converge: when ΣZ​U=0\Sigma_{ZU}=0 the limit is normal even if the selected ranking never settles. In the models of § 3 the mixture is non-normal whenever the correlation is non-zero.

The non-normal component cannot be removed without removing the power. Evaluating each fold through the residual Uk−Γ​ZkU_{k}-\Gamma Z_{k} instead of UkU_{k} would give, after standardization, a standard normal limit for any selection, since this residual is independent of all training moments. Suppose, however, that var⁡(ν∣X)\mathrm{var}(\nu\mid X) is constant and that the alternative is local and linear in the features, τ(x)=τ+m−1/2θTh0(x)\tau(x)=\tau+m^{-1/2}\theta^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}h_{0}(x) with h0=h−E​h​(X)h_{0}=h-Eh(X). In simulations of the model of § 3.1 it rejected about 5% of the time both under the null hypothesis and under two alternatives against which the usual statistic, with normal critical values, rejected 37% and 89% of the time (§ S5.1). Since a signal acts through the non-normal component, § 5 keeps the usual statistic and changes its reference distribution instead.

3 Linear rankings

3.1 One covariate

This section makes the general limit explicit for rankings learned by least squares. We begin with one covariate, where the learner chooses only the sign of a slope, the limits form a one-parameter family, and their shape can be described exactly. The same model satisfies the conditions of a published central limit theorem and is a counterexample to it (§ 3.2). With several covariates (§ 3.3) the learner chooses a direction, and the limit moves towards normality while its variance stays inflated.

Let XX and ε\varepsilon be independent standard normal variables, Y⁡(1)=Y⁡(0)=εY(1)=Y(0)=\varepsilon, assign half of the units to treatment by complete randomization, and split each arm at random into KK folds. The ranking applied to fold kk orders units by β^(k)​x\hat{\beta}_{(k)}x, where β^(k)\hat{\beta}_{(k)} is the least-squares slope, without intercept, of Y~=2​(2​A−1)​ε\tilde{Y}=2(2A-1)\varepsilon on XX in the other K−1K-1 folds. The learner is consistent, β^(k)=Op(m−1/2)\hat{\beta}_{(k)}=O_{p}(m^{-1/2}), but its sign does not converge. Since the denominator of the slope is positive, its sign is that of the sum of the training moments of the other folds, and this is the case h⁡(x)=xh(x)=x, J=1J=1, g1​(x)=sign​(x)g_{1}(x)=\mathrm{sign}(x) and ω⁡(z)=sign⁡(z)\omega(z)=\mathrm{sign}(z) of § 2.2. The training moment of a fold averages X​Y~X\tilde{Y} and its evaluation moment averages sign⁡(X)​Y~\mathrm{sign}(X)\tilde{Y}, so their correlation is ρ=E⁡{X​sign​(X)}=E​|X|=(2/π)1/2\rho=E\{X\mathrm{sign}(X)\}=E|X|=(2/\pi)^{1/2}. The next result describes the distribution of TK​(ρ)T_{K}(\rho) and, for two folds, gives it in closed form.

Proposition 2.

Part (i) follows from Proposition 1, and the proofs of (ii) and (iii) are in the Appendix. Part (i) separates two components. The part of the evaluation moments that is uncorrelated with the training moments contributes the exactly normal variable WW; all departure from normality comes from BKB_{K}, whose distribution depends only on the number of folds, and ρ\rho is its weight in the statistic. The characteristic function (5) takes negative values, for example −0.039-0.039 at t=2t=2 when ρ=(2/π)1/2\rho=(2/\pi)^{1/2}, so T2​(ρ)T_{2}(\rho) is not a scale mixture of centred normal distributions, whose characteristic functions are positive. By (iii), least squares on a normal covariate, with ρ=0.798\rho=0.798, has a bimodal two-fold limit with modes at ±0.59\pm 0.59, whereas the estimated effect in the upper half, with ρ=π−1/2=0.564\rho=\pi^{-1/2}=0.564, has a unimodal one (Fig. 1(a)). Evaluated numerically on a fine grid of ρ\rho, fρf_{\rho} has two modes when |ρ|>ρ∗|\rho|>\rho_{*} and one otherwise. With K=2K=2 and ρ=(2/π)1/2\rho=(2/\pi)^{1/2}, normal critical values reject 8.8% of the time at the nominal 5% level, and normal critical values scaled by the exact standard deviation reject 3.7% (Fig. 1(b)): the limit is more dispersed than the standard error suggests, but its tails are lighter than those of a normal distribution with the same variance.

As KK grows, the excess of the variance (4) over one grows like ρ2​(2​K)1/2/π\rho^{2}(2K)^{1/2}/\pi, so the ratio of the usual standard error to the true standard deviation decays like K−1/4K^{-1/4}: it is 0.84, 0.79 and 0.73 for K=2K=2, 5 and 10. The limit also becomes skewed to the left. When the training moments of all folds nearly sum to zero, ∑r≠kZr≈−Zk\sum_{r\neq k}Z_{r}\approx-Z_{k} for every kk, so each fold is ranked against the sign of its own training moment and all KK terms of (3) tend to be negative together. The two modes move apart as KK grows, to −3.75-3.75 and 0.700.70 for K=50K=50, and a symmetric 5% rejection region then has almost all of its probability in the left tail (Table S2).

The case ρ=1\rho=1 arises in practice: after rescaling, it is the limit of the two-fold cross U-statistic of Kim and Ramdas (2024), and it is the limit of a test in common use. The best linear predictor test of Chernozhukov et al. (2025) regresses the transformed outcome of a fold on its learned score. With a least-squares score on one covariate, the cross-fitted version takes each fold’s own training moment, with the sign of the slope learned on the other folds, and divides it by its standard error. The evaluation moment of a fold is then its training moment, and the limit is BK=TK​(1)B_{K}=T_{K}(1). As the proof of Proposition 2(ii) in the Appendix shows, |B2||B_{2}| is the larger of two independent half-normal variables, so the two-fold test with normal critical values rejects with probability 1−(1−α)21-(1-\alpha)^{2}, which is 9.75% at α=0.05\alpha=0.05; in our simulations it rejected 9.6% of the time with two folds and 13.5% with five, and joint calibration 4.9–5.0% (§ 6.1).

3.2 A published central limit theorem

Theorem 6 of Imai and Li (2025a) asserts that the cross-fitted group effect, standardized by its true variance, is asymptotically normal. The model of § 3.1 satisfies each of its conditions as they are stated: Table S5 of the Supplementary Material sets them out one by one. In brief, the units are independent and identically distributed without interference, treatment is completely randomized with the same number of treated units in every fold, the potential outcomes are standard normal, and because no unit has an effect, the continuity condition on the effect along the score and the stability condition, Assumption 7, hold with every quantity identically zero. By Theorem 2 the standardized θ^+\hat{\theta}_{+} is not asymptotically normal, so the model is a counterexample. Their Assumption 7 requires that, for every a<ba<b,

‖E⁡{Y⁡(1)−Y⁡(0)∣a≤s𝒯​(X)≤b}‖L2​(𝒯)=o⁡(m−1),\bigl\|E\{Y(1)-Y(0)\mid a\leq s_{\mathcal{T}}(X)\leq b\}\bigr\|_{L^{2}(\mathcal{T})}=o(m^{-1}),

where s𝒯s_{\mathcal{T}} is the score learned on a training sample 𝒯\mathcal{T}; here the left-hand side is identically zero. The step of their proof that fails, in their Supplementary Material S9, uses this assumption to replace the group indicators of the learned ranking by those of a fixed ranking. The assumption controls the mean effect within groups, whereas the replacement needs m1/2​Pk​{(g^k−g0)​(Y~−τ)}m^{1/2}P_{k}\{(\hat{g}_{k}-g^{0})(\tilde{Y}-\tau)\}, the difference between the evaluation moments under the learned weight and under a fixed weight g0g^{0}, to vanish. With g0​(x)=sign​(x)g^{0}(x)=\mathrm{sign}(x), the conditional second moment of this term given the training folds is 1616 when the learned slope is negative, which happens with probability one half (Lemma S2). No other fixed weight does better: the learned weight is sign⁡(x)\mathrm{sign}(x) or −sign⁡(x)-\mathrm{sign}(x) with probability one half each, and a fixed weight differs from at least one of the two on a set of positive probability. Close scores need not give close rankings: ss and c​scs rank units identically for c>0c>0, but two slopes that both shrink to zero with opposite signs swap the groups.

The stability conditions of Austern and Zhou (2025) and Bayle et al. (2020), which bound the change in the evaluated loss when the training sample changes, fail for the same reason. The central limit theorem of Bayle et al. (2020) assumes that replacing one training point changes the centred loss by o⁡(σn2/n)o(\sigma_{n}^{2}/n) in mean square, where σn2\sigma_{n}^{2} is the variance of the loss averaged over training samples. Here that average is zero, so σn2=0\sigma_{n}^{2}=0, while replacing one training point flips the sign of the slope with positive probability.

3.3 Several covariates

With several covariates the learner chooses a direction instead of a sign, and the question is how much of the behaviour of § 3.1 survives. Let X∼N⁡(0,Id)X\sim N(0,I_{d}) in the model of that section, and let the ranking applied to fold kk be the least-squares score learned on the other folds. The training moment ZkZ_{k} is now a vector in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and the ranking depends on it only through the direction bk=Sk/|Sk|b_{k}=S_{k}/|S_{k}| of the fitted coefficients, where Sk=∑r≠kZrS_{k}=\sum_{r\neq k}Z_{r}. With Z1,…,ZKZ_{1},\ldots,Z_{K} independent N⁡(0,Id)N(0,I_{d}) vectors and WW a standard normal variable independent of them, let

The proof in § S2.6 rests on the decomposition of Proposition 1: the part of the evaluation moments that is uncorrelated with the training moments contributes an exactly normal variable with variance 1−ρ21-\rho^{2}, so all non-normality lies in BK,dB_{K,d}, and two Gaussian integrations by parts give (7).

Parts (iii) and (iv) carry the practical message, and parts (i) and (ii) qualify it. By (iv), with many covariates the limit is close to normal but its variance is 1+ρ21+\rho^{2}, not one; by (iii), adding folds does not remove this excess once there are three or more covariates. By (i) and (ii), normality is nevertheless never exact, and with two folds the tails are lighter than normal for every dd. Fig. 2 shows the two regimes that result. With one covariate the learner has only a sign to choose, the limit is a mixture over signs, and its variance grows without bound as folds are added. With many covariates each training fold changes the direction only slightly and these changes average out: the variance tends to 1+ρ21+\rho^{2} for every KK, the ratio of the usual standard error to the true standard deviation is (1+ρ2)−1/2=0.78(1+\rho^{2})^{-1/2}=0.78, and the limit is nearly normal. At K=2K=2 the excess kurtosis falls from −0.51-0.51 with one covariate to −0.10-0.10 with sixteen, and normal critical values scaled by the exact standard deviation reject 3.7% and 4.9% of the time. Every limit we computed with two or more covariates is unimodal.

4 Consequences for standard inference

4.1 Variance corrections

Two repairs suggest themselves: inflating the sample variance of the fold estimates, and dividing by the exact standard deviation. Let ψ^k\hat{\psi}_{k} be the estimate from fold kk alone, ψ^\hat{\psi} their mean and S2S^{2} their sample variance. Nadeau and Bengio (2003) replace S2/KS^{2}/K by (1/K+q)​S2(1/K+q)S^{2}, where qq is the ratio of the sizes of the test and training sets, to account for overlapping training sets; under leave-one-fold-out q=1/(K−1)q=1/(K-1). If the ψ^k\hat{\psi}_{k} have a common variance and pairwise correlation rr, then E⁡(S2)=(1−r)​var​(ψ^1)E(S^{2})=(1-r)\mathrm{var}(\hat{\psi}_{1}) and var⁡(ψ^)={1+(K−1)​r}​var​(ψ^1)/K\mathrm{var}(\hat{\psi})=\{1+(K-1)r\}\mathrm{var}(\hat{\psi}_{1})/K, so

E⁡{(1/K+q)​S2}var⁡(ψ^)=(1+K​q)​(1−r)1+(K−1)​r,\frac{E\{(1/K+q)S^{2}\}}{\mathrm{var}(\hat{\psi})}=\frac{(1+Kq)(1-r)}{1+(K-1)r}, (8)

which equals one only if r=q/(1+q)=1/Kr=q/(1+q)=1/K. With one covariate, r=2​ρ2/{π​(2​K−3)1/2}r=2\rho^{2}/\{\pi(2K-3)^{1/2}\} by Theorem 2, so the correction overstates the variance when 4​ρ4​K2<π2​(2​K−3)4\rho^{4}K^{2}<\pi^{2}(2K-3) and understates it otherwise: it is conservative with few folds and anti-conservative with many. As d→∞d\to\infty, r→ρ2/(K−1)r\to\rho^{2}/(K-1) by Proposition 3, and the correction overstates the variance whenever ρ2<(K−1)/K\rho^{2}<(K-1)/K, which holds for every K≥3K\geq 3 when ρ2=2/π\rho^{2}=2/\pi. The paired tt-test, with q=0q=0, always understates the variance when r>0r>0. Dividing by the exact standard deviation restores the level as dd grows but not for d=1d=1, where the rejection rate lies between 3.3% at K=5K=5 and 8.0% at K=50K=50 (Fig. 2(b) and Table 1). No variance correction repairs a non-normal limit.

With many covariates the limit is close to normal, and its variance can be estimated without refitting. By Proposition 1, the evaluation moment of fold kk has conditional variance 1−ρk21-\rho_{k}^{2} given the training moments, where ρk2\rho_{k}^{2} is the squared multiple correlation between the evaluation moment of the selected ranking and the training moment of the fold, and by Proposition 3(iv) the variance of the limit tends to 1+ρ21+\rho^{2} as dd grows. We estimate ρk2\rho_{k}^{2} by the squared multiple correlation between the contributions g^k​(Xi)​ν^i\hat{g}_{k}(X_{i})\hat{\nu}_{i} and {h⁡(Xi)−h¯}​ν^i\{h(X_{i})-\bar{h}\}\hat{\nu}_{i} of the units to the two moments, with ν^i=Y~i−Qn\hat{\nu}_{i}=\tilde{Y}_{i}-Q_{n} and covariances computed within arms, and divide TnT_{n} by (1+ρ¯ 2)1/2(1+\bar{\rho}^{\,2})^{1/2}, where ρ¯ 2\bar{\rho}^{\,2} is the average of the estimates over folds. With one covariate this correction is conservative, since the excess variance 2​ρ2​(K−1)/{π​(2​K−3)1/2}2\rho^{2}(K-1)/\{\pi(2K-3)^{1/2}\} is below ρ2\rho^{2} for K≤5K\leq 5 and the limit has light tails; § 6.3 shows that it restores the level with all covariates of two experiments.

4.2 Local alternatives

Away from the null hypothesis two things change: the learned ranking begins to follow the signal as well as the noise, and the quantity that the test estimates depends on which ranking was learned. To see both in the simplest case, keep two folds and one covariate, and let Y⁡(0)=ε−θm​X/2Y(0)=\varepsilon-\theta_{m}X/2 and Y⁡(1)=ε+θm​X/2Y(1)=\varepsilon+\theta_{m}X/2, so that τ⁡(x)=θm​x\tau(x)=\theta_{m}x; let δm=m1/2​θm/2\delta_{m}=m^{1/2}\theta_{m}/2, the slope divided by the standard error of its estimate from one fold, and c=E​|X|=(2/π)1/2c=E|X|=(2/\pi)^{1/2}. With sk=sign⁡(β^k)s_{k}=\mathrm{sign}(\hat{\beta}_{k}), the group difference of the learned rankings is Δmlearn=θm​c​(s1+s2)\Delta^{\rm learn}_{m}=\theta_{m}c(s_{1}+s_{2}), and its average over training samples is Δmalg=2​θm​c​E​(s1)\Delta^{\rm alg}_{m}=2\theta_{m}c\,E(s_{1}). For finite δ\delta, let skδ=sign⁡(Zk+δ)s_{k}^{\delta}=\mathrm{sign}(Z_{k}+\delta), s¯=2​Φ​(δ)−1\bar{s}=2\Phi(\delta)-1,

Rδ=2−1/2(s2δU1+s1δU2),Aδ=Rδ+2−1/2δc(s1δ+s2δ−2s¯),R_{\delta}=2^{-1/2}(s_{2}^{\delta}U_{1}+s_{1}^{\delta}U_{2}),\qquad A_{\delta}=R_{\delta}+2^{-1/2}\delta c\,(s_{1}^{\delta}+s_{2}^{\delta}-2\bar{s}),

with (Zk,Uk)(Z_{k},U_{k}) as in (3) and ρ=c\rho=c.

Theorem 3.

(i) If δm→δ∈ℝ\delta_{m}\to\delta\in\mathbb{R}, then n1/2​(Dn−Δmlearn)/4n^{1/2}(D_{n}-\Delta^{\rm learn}_{m})/4 and n1/2​(Dn−Δmalg)/4n^{1/2}(D_{n}-\Delta^{\rm alg}_{m})/4 converge jointly in distribution to RδR_{\delta} and AδA_{\delta}, with convergence of second moments; for every finite δ\delta, neither limit is normal after standardization by its variance, and the two limits differ when δ≠0\delta\neq 0. (ii) If θm\theta_{m} converges to a finite θ∗\theta_{*} and m1/2​|θm|→∞m^{1/2}|\theta_{m}|\to\infty, then for both centrings n1/2​(Dn−Δm)/{16+4​θ∗2​(1−c2)}1/2n^{1/2}(D_{n}-\Delta_{m})/\{16+4\theta_{*}^{2}(1-c^{2})\}^{1/2} converges in distribution to N⁡(0,1)N(0,1). (iii) If θm=2​δ/m1/2\theta_{m}=2\delta/m^{1/2}, the Hellinger affinity between the distributions of the data at δ0\delta_{0} and δ1\delta_{1} tends to exp{−(δ1−δ0)2/4}>0\exp\{-(\delta_{1}-\delta_{0})^{2}/4\}>0, so no estimator of δ\delta is consistent.

In words, part (i) concerns signals of the same order as the sampling error of the slope fitted on one fold, part (ii) signals that dominate it, and part (iii) says that two signals of the first kind give data sets that no procedure can tell apart with certainty, however large the sample. Non-normality is therefore not confined to the null hypothesis: it holds along every sequence of local alternatives, and a learner whose predictions converge need not give a ranking that converges. For such signals the estimate has two natural targets, which differ at first order. The first, Δmlearn\Delta^{\rm learn}_{m}, is the group difference of the two rankings actually applied, and is random because the rankings are; the second, Δmalg\Delta^{\rm alg}_{m}, is its average over training samples, a property of the learning algorithm. Both vanish under the null hypothesis, so the distinction matters for confidence intervals rather than for tests. The normal approximation becomes valid once the signal dominates the sampling error of the slope, but by (iii) the data cannot show whether it does, so neither a large sample nor a consistent learner justifies a normal reference distribution. The bootstrap fails for the same reason at the boundary of a parameter space and for directionally differentiable functionals (Andrews, 2000; Fang and Santos, 2019). Proofs and a figure of the two limiting variances are in § S3.

5 Joint calibration

Proposition 1 shows that the normal approximation should be applied to the training and evaluation moments before the ranking is selected, not to the fold estimates after it. Joint calibration does this by a parametric bootstrap of the moments, in three steps, and keeps the usual statistic. First, compute the moments Zk,nZ_{k,n} and Uk,nU_{k,n} of each fold and the statistic TnT_{n} of (1), and estimate Σ\Sigma by the sample covariance Σ^\hat{\Sigma} of the unit-level vectors ViV_{i}, with τ\tau replaced by QnQ_{n}. Second, for b=1,…,Nb=1,\ldots,N, draw independent vectors (Zk∗T,Uk∗T)T∼N⁡(0,Σ^)(Z_{k}^{*{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}},U_{k}^{*{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}})^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}\sim N(0,\hat{\Sigma}) (k=1,…,K)(k=1,\ldots,K) and compute Tb∗T_{b}^{*} from (1) with the draws in place of the moments and Σ^U​U\hat{\Sigma}_{UU} unchanged, so that the draws pass through the same selection function and the same training sets as the data. Third, report the symmetric pp-value p^={1+#(b:|Tb∗|≥|Tn|)}/(N+1)\hat{p}=\{1+\#(b:|T_{b}^{*}|\geq|T_{n}|)\}/(N+1), or the equal-tailed one; Algorithm 1 of the Supplementary Material states the procedure in full and defines both pp-values.

Theorem 4.

Suppose that the conditions of Theorem 1 hold and that Σ^\hat{\Sigma} converges in probability to Σ\Sigma. Let c^α\hat{c}_{\alpha} be the (1−α)(1-\alpha) quantile of |T∗||T^{*}|, where T∗T^{*} is computed as TΣT_{\Sigma} in (2) with Σ^\hat{\Sigma} in place of Σ\Sigma. If the distribution function of |TΣ||T_{\Sigma}| is continuous and strictly increasing at its (1−α)(1-\alpha) quantile, then pr⁡(|Tn|>c^α)→α\mathrm{pr}(|T_{n}|>\hat{c}_{\alpha})\to\alpha under the null hypothesis. The test that rejects when TnT_{n} lies outside the α/2\alpha/2 and 1−α/21-\alpha/2 quantiles of T∗T^{*} has asymptotic level α\alpha when the distribution function of TΣT_{\Sigma} is continuous and strictly increasing at those quantiles.

The symmetric and equal-tailed regions coincide for two folds and an odd selection function, since replacing (Z1,U1)(Z_{1},U_{1}) by (−Z1,−U1)(-Z_{1},-U_{1}) maps TΣT_{\Sigma} to −TΣ-T_{\Sigma}. With more folds TΣT_{\Sigma} is skewed to the left while a signal shifts TnT_{n} to the right, so the symmetric region has most of its probability in the tail that a signal does not reach; with K=50K=50 in the model of § 3.1, a signal that the equal-tailed test detects 25.7% of the time is detected 1.8% of the time by the symmetric one. We therefore recommend the equal-tailed region whenever K>2K>2. When the numbers of treated units in each fold are fixed, Σ\Sigma is replaced by a covariance computed within arms (§ S4.3). With heavy-tailed outcomes the sample covariance may be replaced by a robust estimator (Ledoit and Wolf, 2004; Wei and Minsker, 2017; Ke et al., 2019; He and Yan, 2026); Theorem 4 requires only that the estimator be consistent. The test needs one pass through the data and no refitting: with q=d+Jq=d+J, its cost is of order n​q2+q3+N​K​q2nq^{2}+q^{3}+NKq^{2}, whereas a randomization test refits the learner for every draw of the treatment labels, and rank-transformed subsampling (Guo and Shah, 2025), which applies to a wider class of procedures, refits it on every subsample.

6 Numerical results

6.1 Simulations

We simulated the model of § 3.1 with n=6000n=6000, splitting each fold at its empirical median. Table 1 compares five reference distributions for the same statistic. Normal critical values with the usual standard error over-reject more as folds are added, in line with the rejection rates 8.8%, 11.0% and 15.1% implied by the limits of Theorem 2 for K=2K=2, 5 and 10. The correction of Nadeau and Bengio (2003) holds the level up to K=10K=10 and over-rejects from K=20K=20, as (8) predicts, and where it holds the level it has little power. Normal critical values scaled by the exact standard deviation under-reject at small KK and over-reject at K=50K=50. Joint calibration, with the covariance estimated in each replication, rejects 4.5–5.1% at every KK, and its equal-tailed version keeps its power as KK grows. The variance and kurtosis of the statistic are close to those of its limit, and the critical value of the limit holds the level with as few as 200 units (§ S5.1).

Table 2 compares joint calibration, on the same data sets, with two reference distributions that refit the rankings: a randomization test, which redraws the treatment labels within folds 499 times, refits the rankings for every draw and is exact under the sharp null hypothesis of no effect on any unit, and rank-transformed subsampling (Guo and Shah, 2025), which refits them on 800 subsamples of size n/log⁡nn/\log n. All three held the level at every KK, rejecting 4.3–5.6% of the time. Their power depended on the rejection region more than on the method: with the symmetric region all three lost power as KK grew, for the reason given in § 5, whereas with equal tails joint calibration and the randomization test kept about 25% power at every KK. Per data set, joint calibration took 2–4 milliseconds, the randomization test about 0.4 seconds and subsampling about 0.2 seconds. Each refit here is a closed-form slope; for a learner that is expensive to fit, the last two times grow with the cost of a fit and the first does not.

Table 3 varies the setting, with two and five folds: binary outcomes; tt-distributed errors with three degrees of freedom; 200 units; a fifth of the units treated; individual effects that vary while the conditional average effect is constant, so that the sharp null hypothesis fails; five covariates, of which the median split with the largest absolute training moment is selected, with the sign of that moment; and the best linear predictor test of § 3.1. Normal critical values rejected 8.6–13.5% of the time and the correction of Nadeau and Bengio (2003) 3.5–5.2%, while joint calibration rejected 3.9–5.9% and the randomization test 4.1–6.2%. With varying individual effects the randomization test is not exact, but it still held the level, as studentized permutation tests often do under weak null hypotheses (Chung and Romano, 2013).

6.2 An e-mail experiment

The Hillstrom experiment randomized customers to a men’s e-mail, a women’s e-mail or none (Hillstrom, 2008a; Hillstrom, 2008b). We compare the men’s e-mail with no e-mail for 42 613 customers, with a website visit within two weeks as outcome, and rank customers by the logarithm of one plus their spending in the past year: each of two folds learns a least-squares slope and ranks the other. The standardized statistic is 2.11. Treating the folds as independent gives a two-sided pp-value of 0.035, whereas joint calibration gives 0.065, and rank-transformed subsampling, at a much higher computational cost, gives 0.054–0.064. The reference distributions disagree because the training and evaluation moments of each fold have correlation about 0.85. Two fold statistics with such correlations ρ1\rho_{1} and ρ2\rho_{2} have correlation 2​ρ1​ρ2/π2\rho_{1}\rho_{2}/\pi in the limit, here 0.46, and the correlation observed across subsamples is the same. With five and ten folds the normal pp-values are 0.047 and 0.029, and the equal-tailed joint pp-values 0.092 and 0.057. To check which reference distribution is appropriate for these data, we redrew the e-mail labels 2000 times, so that the labels have no effect on any customer, and repeated the analysis: normal critical values rejected 8.8%, 11.0% and 16.8% of the time with two, five and ten folds, and joint calibration 4.5–5.0% (§ S5.3).

6.3 Experiments with redrawn treatment labels

To see the two regimes of Proposition 3 on real covariates, we kept the covariates and outcomes of two experiments and redrew the treatment labels, so that no unit has an effect and every rejection is false. In the ACTG 175 trial (Hammer et al., 1996a; Hammer et al., 1996b), 1054 patients received zidovudine or zidovudine plus didanosine; the outcome is the change in CD4 count and there are 16 baseline covariates. From the Criteo uplift data (Diemert et al., 2018a; Diemert et al., 2018b) we took 20 000 rows with 12 features and a website visit as outcome. With a least-squares ranking on a single covariate the statistic had clearly negative excess kurtosis, and the test standardized by its exact standard deviation was conservative; with all covariates the statistic was close to normal, as Proposition 3 predicts, and the same test had the nominal level. When the ranking is selected from a finite set of median splits, by the largest absolute training moment and with its sign, Theorem 4 applies: joint calibration rejected 4.5–5.9% of the time, where normal critical values rejected 8.6–13.2%. For least squares of the transformed outcome on all covariates, the correction of § 4.1 rejected 3.2–5.2% of the time, where normal critical values rejected 10.7–13.4%; with a single covariate it was conservative, as expected (§ S5.4).

7 Discussion

Four questions remain open. First, joint calibration draws a vector of moments of fixed, finite dimension. Rankings learned from infinite classes, such as least squares on many covariates or a random forest, at present need a reference distribution that refits the learner, as rank-transformed subsampling and the randomization test do; a calibration of such rankings without refitting would be useful. The correction of § 4.1 is one for least squares on many covariates, but its justification rests on the Gaussian model of Proposition 3 and has yet to be extended to other covariate distributions. Second, under local alternatives the group effect of the learned ranking and its average over training samples differ at first order, and uniform inference for the latter cannot rely on an estimate of the signal, which by Theorem 3(iii) cannot be estimated consistently. Third, our limits hold the numbers of candidate rankings, covariates and folds fixed as the sample grows. The order of the limits matters: with one covariate, TK​(ρ)T_{K}(\rho) converges in distribution to a skew-normal distribution as K→∞K\to\infty, but its variance diverges like K1/2K^{1/2}, so its moments do not converge, and the rejection rate of the test standardized by the exact standard deviation is not monotone in KK (Table 1). With one unit per fold, K=nK=n, there is neither a central limit theorem nor a median within a fold, and neither Theorem 1 nor joint calibration applies. Fourth, the statistic is often averaged over repeated partitions. Methods that combine split-sample statistics (Meinshausen et al., 2009; DiCiccio et al., 2020; Ritzwoller and Romano, 2026) take as inputs single-partition statistics with known reference distributions, which joint calibration supplies, but the distribution of the average over partitions has not been described.

Appendix S2 Asymptotic distributions

S2.1 Conditional centring

Let 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k} be the σ\sigma-field generated by the fold labels, any randomness of the learner, all data outside fold kk and the covariates of fold kk.

Lemma S1 (Conditional centring).

Suppose that the ranking weight g^k\widehat{g}_{k} that evaluates fold kk is determined by the treatments and outcomes of the folds in F⁡(k)F(k), the covariates of all folds, the fold labels and the learner’s randomness. Then, for i∈Iki\in I_{k}, E⁡[g^k​(Xi)​Y~i∣𝒢k]=g^k​(Xi)​τ​(Xi)E[\widehat{g}_{k}(X_{i})\tilde{Y}_{i}\mid\mathcal{G}_{k}]=\widehat{g}_{k}(X_{i})\tau(X_{i}), and these products are conditionally independent across the units of fold kk. Under HτH_{\tau}, if the weights sum to zero over the fold, Dk=2​Pk​(g^k​Y~)D_{k}=2P_{k}(\widehat{g}_{k}\tilde{Y}) has conditional mean zero.

Proof.

The weight g^k\widehat{g}_{k} is 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}-measurable: it uses treatments and outcomes only from the folds in F⁡(k)F(k), and covariates, including those of fold kk through the empirical median. Given 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}, the pairs (Ai,Yi)(A_{i},Y_{i}), i∈Iki\in I_{k}, are independent, and randomization gives E⁡(Y~i∣𝒢k)=E⁡(Y~i∣Xi)=τ⁡(Xi)E(\tilde{Y}_{i}\mid\mathcal{G}_{k})=E(\tilde{Y}_{i}\mid X_{i})=\tau(X_{i}). Under HτH_{\tau} the conditional mean of DkD_{k} is 2​τ​Pk​g^k2\tau P_{k}\widehat{g}_{k}, which is zero when the weights sum to zero. ∎

S2.2 Proof of Theorem 2 for two folds

Step 1: the assignment and the moments. Condition on the assignment and on the split of each arm into folds. The assignment is independent of the potential outcomes and covariates, and the units are independent and identically distributed, so the units can be relabelled by fold and arm, and the pairs (Xi,εi)(X_{i},\varepsilon_{i}) remain independent with the distribution (S5). Since εi\varepsilon_{i} is symmetric about zero, the variables ξi=(2​Ai−1)​εi\xi_{i}=(2A_{i}-1)\varepsilon_{i} are, given the assignment, independent standard normal and independent of the XiX_{i}, and Y~i=2​ξi\tilde{Y}_{i}=2\xi_{i}.

The moments (S7) are standardized sums of the independent vectors

1m1/2​∑i∈Ik(ξi,Xi​ξi,sign⁡(Xi)​ξi)T,\frac{1}{{m}^{1/2}}\sum_{i\in I_{k}}(\xi_{i},\ X_{i}\xi_{i},\ \mathrm{sign}(X_{i})\xi_{i})^{{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}},

with mean zero and covariance

(10001(2/π)1/20(2/π)1/21).\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&(2/\pi)^{1/2}\\ 0&(2/\pi)^{1/2}&1\end{pmatrix}. (S23)

The multivariate central limit theorem gives joint convergence within each fold, and the two folds are independent. The conditional distribution given the assignment does not depend on which units are treated, so the same limit holds unconditionally. For the same reason, simulations in which the treated units are fixed have the distribution of the statistic under complete randomization.

Step 2: replacing the empirical median. Let Nk+=∑i∈Ik1{Xi>0}N_{k}^{+}=\sum_{i\in I_{k}}1\{X_{i}>0\}. Because XX is continuous, the empirical upper half of fold kk and the population upper half differ in exactly

units. Write

Given the covariates of the fold, RkR_{k} has mean zero and only CkC_{k} non-zero coefficients, each of absolute value 2. Hence

where the last inequality uses Nk+∼Binomial⁡(m,1/2)N_{k}^{+}\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(m,1/2) and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. Multiplying by the sign learned in the other fold does not change the absolute value of the remainder, and the sum of the remainders over finitely many folds is op​(1)o_{p}(1); no independence between the remainders of the two folds is used.

The limit ZkZ_{k} is standard normal, so it equals zero with probability zero and the sign function is almost surely continuous at it. Lemma S3 (First-order expansion of the sample moments).

Under HτH_{\tau}, (S14) and the quantile conditions above, the moments (S15) satisfy (S16). The sample covariance of the unit-level vectors is consistent for Σ\Sigma whenever τ^→τ\widehat{\tau}\to\tau. A median on the boundary of an atom satisfies neither condition and is not covered by the lemma.

S4.2 Proofs of Theorems 1 and 4

The folds are disjoint sets of independent rows, so the raw sums of different folds are independent. The expansion (S16), the multivariate central limit theorem and this independence give

((Z1,n,U1,n),…,(ZK,n,UK,n))→((Z1,U1),…,(ZK,UK)),((Z_{1,n},U_{1,n}),\ldots,(Z_{K,n},U_{K,n}))\to((Z_{1},U_{1}),\ldots,(Z_{K},U_{K})),

where the limits are the independent N⁡(0,Σ)N(0,\Sigma) vectors of Theorem 1. Consider the map

ℱ⁡((z1,u1),…,(zK,uK),Σ)=∑k=1KωkT​uk(∑k=1KωkT​ΣU​U​ωk)1/2,ωk=ω⁡(∑r∈F⁡(k)zr).\mathcal{F}((z_{1},u_{1}),\ldots,(z_{K},u_{K});\Sigma)=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\omega_{k}^{{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}}u_{k}}{\big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\omega_{k}^{{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}}\Sigma_{UU}\omega_{k}\big)^{1/2}},\qquad\omega_{k}=\omega\left(\sum_{r\in F(k)}z_{r}\right).

The sets F⁡(k)F(k) are fixed. The map is continuous in Σ\Sigma, and it can be discontinuous in its other arguments only where the selection function is discontinuous at one of the KK sums of training moments. By assumption the limiting vector lies at such a point with probability zero, and the denominator is positive almost surely. Since Σ^n→Σ\widehat{\Sigma}_{n}\to\Sigma, the continuous mapping theorem gives the limit (2). Only almost-sure continuity is used, so the selection function may be discontinuous on any set to which the sums of training moments assign probability zero. When folds jj and kk train each other, j∈F⁡(k)j\in F(k) and k∈F⁡(j)k\in F(j), the selection ω⁡(∑r∈F⁡(k)Zr)\omega(\sum_{r\in F(k)}Z_{r}) depends on ZjZ_{j}, which is correlated with UjU_{j}; this dependence is kept by the map and is the source of the non-normal limit.

For the reference distribution with an estimated covariance, we use the continuity of the symmetric square root of a positive semidefinite matrix. With independent standard normal vectors ζ1,…,ζK\zeta_{1},\ldots,\zeta_{K}, write the reference vectors as Σ^n1/2​ζk\widehat{\Sigma}_{n}^{1/2}\zeta_{k}. Every subsequence has a further subsequence along which Σ^n→Σ\widehat{\Sigma}_{n}\to\Sigma almost surely, and along it the reference vectors converge almost surely to Σ1/2​ζk\Sigma^{1/2}\zeta_{k}. The map is almost surely continuous at the limit, so for every bounded continuous test function bb, dominated convergence gives

E⁡{b⁡(Tn∗)∣data}⟶E​b​(TΣ)E\{b(T_{n}^{*})\mid\text{data}\}\longrightarrow Eb(T_{\Sigma})

almost surely. Since this holds along a further subsequence of every subsequence, the conditional distribution of Tn∗T_{n}^{*} converges weakly to the distribution of TΣT_{\Sigma}, in probability. The same proof applies when a separate consistent covariance estimator is used for each fold.

For the reference distribution of the absolute value, weak convergence and the stated quantile condition give consistency of the (1−α)(1-\alpha) quantile. Conditionally on the data, the NN draws are independent, so as N→∞N\to\infty their empirical distribution function converges uniformly, in probability, to the conditional distribution function of |T∗||T^{*}|. The empirical critical value therefore satisfies c^α,n→cα\widehat{c}_{\alpha,n}\to c_{\alpha}. Finally, |Tn|→|TΣ||T_{n}|\to|T_{\Sigma}|, the absence of an atom at the critical value and Slutsky’s theorem give the first statement of Theorem 4. For the equal-tailed region, the same argument applied to the distribution of TΣT_{\Sigma} itself gives consistency of the empirical α/2\alpha/2 and 1−α/21-\alpha/2 quantiles, and Tn→TΣT_{n}\to T_{\Sigma} gives the level. If each fold is standardized separately instead of through the common denominator, only the map ℱ\mathcal{F} changes and the argument applies as it stands.

S4.3 Fixed arm sizes

Suppose that the units are sampled independently from a population and that treatment is assigned by complete randomization with a fixed number of treated units in each fold; take pp in (S1) to be the treated proportion. Let VaV_{a} be the vector (S13) for a unit in arm aa. The covariance in the joint central limit theorem is

Σdes=p​cov​(V1)+(1−p)​cov​(V0),\Sigma_{\mathrm{des}}=p\mathrm{cov}(V_{1})+(1-p)\mathrm{cov}(V_{0}), (S38)

estimated by centring within each arm and weighting the arms by their proportions. It is related to the covariance Σiid\Sigma_{\mathrm{iid}} under independent Bernoulli assignment by

Σiid=Σdes+p⁡(1−p)​(E​V1−E​V0)​(E​V1−E​V0)T.\Sigma_{\mathrm{iid}}=\Sigma_{\mathrm{des}}+p(1-p)(EV_{1}-EV_{0})(EV_{1}-EV_{0})^{{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}}. (S39)

The expansion (S16) still holds under HτH_{\tau}, because the means of the two arms, weighted by their proportions, cancel, as shown below. Theorem 4 therefore holds with Σdes\Sigma_{\mathrm{des}} in place of Σ\Sigma. For cluster-randomized or stratified experiments, Σ\Sigma must be replaced by the limiting covariance under the design actually used.

Proof. Let the treated share of every fold equal a fixed pp, with mam_{a} units in arm aa of each fold and m1/m=pm_{1}/m=p. Given the assignment and the split into folds, and after relabelling, the two arms are independent samples from their respective populations. Write Pk,aP_{k,a} for the mean within arm aa of fold kk, PaP_{a} for the population distribution of that arm, Y~a\tilde{Y}_{a} and νa=Y~a−τ\nu_{a}=\tilde{Y}_{a}-\tau for the transformed outcome and its centred version in arm aa, and p1=pp_{1}=p, p0=1−pp_{0}=1-p. Under HτH_{\tau},

∑a=01pa​Pa​Va=0,\sum_{a=0}^{1}p_{a}P_{a}V_{a}=0,

so

1m1/2∑a=01∑i∈Ik:Ai=aVa,i=∑a=01(pa)1/21(ma)1/2∑i∈Ik:Ai=a(Va,i−PaVa).\frac{1}{{m}^{1/2}}\sum_{a=0}^{1}\sum_{i\in I_{k}:A_{i}=a}V_{a,i}=\sum_{a=0}^{1}(p_{a})^{1/2}\,\frac{1}{(m_{a})^{1/2}}\sum_{i\in I_{k}:A_{i}=a}(V_{a,i}-P_{a}V_{a}). (S40)

Independent central limit theorems within the arms give (S38), and the population decomposition of the covariance gives (S39). Consistency of the within-arm sample covariance follows from the law of large numbers for second moments in each arm and the plug-in control in the proof of Lemma S3.

Within an arm, E⁡(νa∣X)E(\nu_{a}\mid X) is not zero, so the argument of Lemma S3 cannot be applied arm by arm. The means cancel only when the two arms are combined: for any bounded weight vv that depends only on XX, randomization and HτH_{\tau} give

∑a=01pa​Pa​[v⁡(X)​νa]=E⁡[v⁡(X)​{τ⁡(X)−τ}]=0.\sum_{a=0}^{1}p_{a}P_{a}[v(X)\nu_{a}]=E[v(X)\{\tau(X)-\tau\}]=0. (S41)

Identity (S41) holds for every such weight, and hence for the data-dependent weight v=g^−gv=\widehat{g}-g, so replacing the population median by the empirical one does not change the mean. What remains is a sum of empirical processes centred within each arm:

m1/2​Pk​[(g^−g)​ν]=m1/2​∑apa​(Pk,a−Pa)​[(g^−g)​νa].{m}^{1/2}P_{k}[(\widehat{g}-g)\nu]={m}^{1/2}\sum_{a}p_{a}(P_{k,a}-P_{a})[(\widehat{g}-g)\nu_{a}].

Under condition (i) of § S4.1, {νa​1​(sj≤t):t∈ℝ}\{\nu_{a}1(s_{j}\leq t):t\in\mathbb{R}\} is a Vapnik–Chervonenkis class with a square-integrable envelope, so the empirical process indexed by it is asymptotically equicontinuous in the L2​(Pa)L^{2}(P_{a}) distance (van der Vaart and Wellner, 1996). Consistency of the empirical median, the absence of an atom and Pa​νa2<∞P_{a}\nu_{a}^{2}<\infty imply that the L2​(Pa)L^{2}(P_{a}) distance between the indicators at the empirical and population medians tends to zero, so the remainder is op​(1)o_{p}(1). Under condition (ii), the argument in the proof of Lemma S3 applies: the error of λ^k,j\widehat{\lambda}_{k,j} multiplies a centred sum that is Op​(1)O_{p}(1).

If the treated proportion of fold kk is pk=p+O⁡(m−1)p_{k}=p+O(m^{-1}), the coefficients 1/pk1/p_{k} and 1/(1−pk)1/(1-p_{k}) of the transformed outcome differ from those at pp by O⁡(m−1)O(m^{-1}), which changes the sums standardized by m1/2m^{1/2} by op​(1)o_{p}(1) under the moment conditions. Fold sizes that differ by a bounded number of units are covered by the same argument.

Appendix S5 Experiments

S5.1 Simulations in the model of the paper

Unless stated otherwise, the simulations use the model of § 3.1: one standard normal covariate, normal errors, half of each fold treated, and fold kk ranked at its median by the least-squares slope learned on the other folds.

Two folds. Table S6 shows that the statistic is close to its limit with as few as 200 units. Its variance and kurtosis are close to the limiting values 1.405 and 2.489, normal critical values over-reject at every sample size, normal critical values scaled by the limiting standard deviation under-reject, and the critical value of T2T_{2} holds the level. A uniform covariate gives the same picture.

KK folds. Table S7 compares the statistic at n=6000n=6000 with its limit TKT_{K} in variance, kurtosis and rejection rate; the two agree closely.

Variance corrections. Table S8 complements Table 1. The column rr is the correlation between two fold estimates implied by Theorem 2, 1/K1/K is the correlation at which the correction of Nadeau and Bengio is exact, and the ratio is the expected corrected variance over the exact variance, from (8). The correction under-rejects where the ratio is clearly above one and over-rejects where it is below one. At K=10K=10 the ratio is 1.01, yet the corrected test rejects 5.3% of the time, because its rejection rate depends also on the randomness of the variance estimate and on the shape of the limit. With the exact variance, the limit rejects 3.7%, 3.3%, 3.7%, 5.2% and 8.0% of the time for K=2K=2, 5, 10, 20 and 50.

Rejection regions. In the limit, the symmetric 5% region of TKT_{K} has probability 2.5% in each tail for K=2K=2, 4.0% in the left tail and 1.0% in the right for K=10K=10, and 4.95% in the left tail for K=50K=50, where the region is |T|>4.01|T|>4.01 and the equal-tailed region is T<−4.57T<-4.57 or T>2.24T>2.24. A signal shifts the statistic to the right, so the symmetric region loses power as KK grows. Table S9 shows this for n=6000n=6000 and τ⁡(x)=a​x/n1/2\tau(x)=ax/n^{1/2}, both with the quantiles of TKT_{K}, which are unknown in practice, and with joint calibration using the covariance estimated in each data set and 999 draws.

Three folds, three rankings and binary outcomes. Three covariates are independent and uniform on [0,1][0,1]; given XX, Y⁡(0)Y(0) and Y⁡(1)Y(1) are independent Bernoulli variables with means 0.2+0.2​X10.2+0.2X_{1} and 0.3+0.2​X10.3+0.2X_{1}, so the conditional average effect is 0.1 everywhere while individual effects vary. Each fold has as many treated as control units, the candidate rankings are the median splits of the three covariates, and the training moments of the other two folds select a covariate and its sign. Table S10 shows that joint calibration holds the level where normal critical values, which ignore the dependence between folds, do not.

Removing the non-normal component. To illustrate the last paragraph of § 2.4, each fold is also evaluated through Uk−Γ^​ZkU_{k}-\hat{\Gamma}Z_{k}, with Γ^\hat{\Gamma} estimated from the contributions of the units to the two moments, and the resulting statistic is divided by its estimated standard deviation. With n=6000n=6000 and 4000 data sets for each of K=2K=2, 5 and 10, this statistic had variance between 0.98 and 1.02 and rejected 4.8–5.6% of the time under the null hypothesis, as Proposition 1 predicts. Under τ⁡(x)=4​x/n1/2\tau(x)=4x/n^{1/2} and 8​x/n1/28x/n^{1/2} it still rejected 4.8–5.3% of the time, whereas the usual statistic rejected about 37% and 89% of the time with normal critical values.

S5.2 Reference distributions that refit the rankings, and further settings

Design. Each fold has a fixed number of treated units, and the ranking of fold kk is the sign of ∑r≠kZr\sum_{r\neq k}Z_{r} times the median split of the covariate; in the setting with five rankings it is the median split of the covariate with the largest absolute coordinate of ∑r≠kZr\sum_{r\neq k}Z_{r}, with that coordinate’s sign. All tests are two-sided at the 5% level and use the same data sets. Joint calibration estimates Σ\Sigma by (S38) and uses 999 draws.

Randomization test. The treatment labels are redrawn within each fold, keeping its number of treated units, 499 times; for every draw the rankings are refitted and the usual standardized statistic is recomputed, and the symmetric and equal-tailed pp-values are formed as in Algorithm 1. Under the sharp null hypothesis that Yi​(1)=Yi​(0)Y_{i}(1)=Y_{i}(0) for every unit, this test is exact.

Rank-transformed subsampling. Subsamples of about n/log⁡nn/\log n units are formed as in Algorithm 2 of Guo and Shah (2025): the units of each arm are permuted and cut into blocks, and matching blocks of the two arms form one subsample, giving 800 subsamples when n=6000n=6000. Each subsample is split into KK folds balanced by arm, and its fold statistics tk=sign⁡(∑r≠kZr)​Uk/σ^kt_{k}=\mathrm{sign}(\sum_{r\neq k}Z_{r})U_{k}/\widehat{\sigma}_{k} are computed with the within-arm standard deviation σ^k\widehat{\sigma}_{k} of the unit contributions. All fold statistics are ranked jointly and transformed to normal scores, the scores of each subsample are summed and divided by K1/2K^{1/2}, and the full-sample statistic of the same form is compared with these sums in absolute value.

Best linear predictor. Fold kk regresses Y~\tilde{Y} on its centred covariate; the tt-statistic of the slope, signed by the slope fitted on the other folds, is summed over folds and divided by K1/2K^{1/2}. Joint calibration draws only the training moments, because the evaluation moment of each fold equals its training moment.

Computing time. Times are means per data set with n=6000n=6000 and include computing the statistic. A refit here is a closed-form slope, so the ratios understate the cost of refitting for learners that are expensive to fit.

S5.3 The Hillstrom analysis

Throughout §§ S5.3 and S5.4, SS denotes the usual standardized statistic of § 2.1.

Data. The experiment randomized 64,000 customers to three arms; we use the 42,613 customers of the men’s e-mail and no-e-mail arms and treat the assignment as complete randomization of independent customers. A visit within two weeks was recorded for 10.6% of control and 18.3% of treated customers. Each arm is split at random into two folds, and both folds learn a positive slope, so both rank customers with higher past spending as the high-effect group.

Two folds. The estimated correlation between the training and evaluation moments is 0.84 in one fold and 0.85 in the other. Joint calibration gives p=0.065p=0.065 and a 5% critical value of 2.22 for the absolute statistic. Rank-transformed subsampling gives 0.054–0.064 for three subsample sizes; here the subsamples are drawn independently within arms rather than as blocks of permutations. Treating the folds as independent gives 0.035. For comparison, the two single-split tests give 0.21 and 0.085 (Bonferroni combination 0.17), the paired tt-test and the correction of Nadeau and Bengio, each with one degree of freedom, give 0.093 and 0.158, and a full-sample test of the linear moment E⁡[{X−E⁡(X)}​(Y~−τ)]=0E[\{X-E(X)\}(\tilde{Y}-\tau)]=0, which weights heterogeneity differently, gives 0.028.

Five and ten folds. Table S11 repeats the analysis with K=5K=5 and 10, each fold ranked by the sign learned on the others; every fold is ranked in the same direction, and the training–evaluation correlations lie between 0.83 and 0.87. The upper quantile of the reference distribution stays near 2.23 while its left tail widens with KK, as in the limit, and at K=10K=10 the equal-tailed pp-value is half the symmetric one.

Redrawn labels. To check the two reference distributions on these data, we keep the covariate and outcome of every customer, redraw the e-mail labels by complete randomization with the observed arm sizes, so that the labels have no effect on any customer, and repeat the analysis on 2000 data sets for each KK. Table S12 gives the rejection rates. The variance of the statistic, 1.46, 1.67 and 1.97, is close to the values 1.46, 1.70 and 2.00 that (4) gives for the observed correlation 0.85.

S5.4 Experiments with redrawn treatment labels

Data and labels. From ACTG 175 (Hammer et al., 1996a; Hammer et al., 1996b) we use the 1054 patients randomized to zidovudine or to zidovudine plus didanosine, with 16 baseline covariates and the change in CD4 count at week 20 as outcome; the trial was stratified by prior antiretroviral therapy, so labels are redrawn and covariances computed within strata. From the Criteo uplift data (Diemert et al., 2018a; Diemert et al., 2018b) we use a uniform sample of 20,000 units with twelve features and a website visit as outcome. In every data set the covariates and outcomes stay fixed and the labels are redrawn by complete randomization with the original numbers in each stratum and arm, so that the labels have no effect on any unit.

One covariate against all covariates. Table S13 compares a least-squares ranking on one covariate with the same ranking on all covariates, under leave-one-fold-out with folds balanced within stratum and arm.

A finite set of rankings. Median splits of continuous covariates, with their sign, are selected by the largest absolute coordinate of the summed training moments: age, weight, days of prior therapy, and CD4 and CD8 counts on ACTG (J=5J=5), and the six Criteo features whose medians lie strictly inside the range of their values (J=6J=6). This setting falls under Theorem 4. Table S14 also reports calibration of the sum Sn=K−1/2∑kω^kTUk,nS_{n}=K^{-1/2}\sum_{k}\hat{\omega}_{k}^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}U_{k,n}, without the standardization by v^\hat{v} in (1), which differs from TnT_{n} when the candidate rankings have different variances.

A correction for many covariates. For the correction of § 4.1, fold kk is ranked by least squares of Y~\tilde{Y} on the covariates, fitted on the other folds, and split at the median of its score. Let ν^i=Y~i−τ^\hat{\nu}_{i}=\tilde{Y}_{i}-\hat{\tau}, and let ti=(Xi−X¯)​ν^it_{i}=(X_{i}-\bar{X})\hat{\nu}_{i} and ek,i=g^k​(Xi)​ν^ie_{k,i}=\hat{g}_{k}(X_{i})\hat{\nu}_{i} be the contributions of unit ii to the training moment and to the evaluation moment under g^k\hat{g}_{k}, the median split of the score of fold kk. Let C^\hat{C} be the covariance matrix of (ti,ek,i)(t_{i},e_{k,i}) over all units, computed within each combination of stratum and arm. Then ρ^k2=c^kT​C^t​t−1​c^k/C^e​e\hat{\rho}_{k}^{2}=\hat{c}_{k}^{\mathrm{\scriptscriptstyle T}}\hat{C}_{tt}^{-1}\hat{c}_{k}/\hat{C}_{ee}, where c^k\hat{c}_{k} is the covariance of tit_{i} and ek,ie_{k,i}, and the corrected statistic is S(1+ρ¯ 2)−1/2S(1+\bar{\rho}^{\,2})^{-1/2} with ρ¯ 2\bar{\rho}^{\,2} the average of ρ^k2\hat{\rho}_{k}^{2} over folds. In Table S15, with all covariates the variance of SS lies within 10% of 1+ρ¯ 21+\bar{\rho}^{\,2}. With one covariate 1+ρ¯ 21+\bar{\rho}^{\,2} exceeds it by up to 16% at K=2K=2, as the variance excess 2​ρ2/π2\rho^{2}/\pi of Theorem 2 predicts, and the light tails make the corrected test conservative at K=5K=5 as well.

Observed labels. With the observed labels, the test based on the finite set of rankings shows no heterogeneity on ACTG 175, whichever reference distribution is used. On Criteo with K=5K=5 the normal pp-value is 0.0025, and joint calibration and a randomization reference both give 0.011 for TnT_{n}; calibrating SnS_{n} instead gives 0.083, because the selected ranking has a small variance and the reference distribution of SnS_{n} is dominated by rankings with larger ones.
